content.title: About
content.content: Black beans and brown rice are a combination of plant protein, complex carbohydrates, and fiber. Beans are rich in protein, iron, and antioxidants, while brown rice retains the bran and germ, making it more nutritious than white rice.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Black beans are often called "young beans" and are a staple in Latin American cuisine.
Brown rice is a whole grain that keeps the bran, germ, and endosperm intact.
Together, beans and rice provide a complete set of essential amino acids, similar to animal protein.
Black beans contain anthocyanins, powerful antioxidants that give them their dark color.
When stored properly, brown rice can stay fresh for up to 6 months in a cool, dry place.

items.title: Rich in plant protein
items.content: Black beans provide about 8 g of protein per 100 g, supporting muscle maintenance.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Both foods supply soluble and insoluble fiber, promoting healthy digestion and blood‑sugar control.

items.title: Source of iron and magnesium
items.content: Black beans are a good source of iron, while brown rice supplies magnesium, important for nerve and muscle function.

items.title: Supports cardiovascular health
items.content: Fiber and antioxidants help lower cholesterol and protect blood vessels from oxidative stress.

items.title: Steady energy source
items.content: Complex carbs in brown rice release glucose slowly, providing lasting satiety.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to beans, ranging from skin rash to anaphylaxis.

items.title: Phytic acid
items.content: Brown rice contains phytic acid, which can reduce mineral absorption if consumed in excess.

items.title: Gas and bloating
items.content: Beans can cause gastrointestinal discomfort in sensitive people; soaking and thorough cooking help.

items.title: Potential gluten cross‑contamination
items.content: People with celiac disease should ensure the rice is not contaminated with gluten during processing.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cook beans and rice together as a side dish, in salads, soups, or as a vegetarian pilaf. Soak beans 8–12 hours, then boil until tender. Cook brown rice 40–45 minutes in a 1:2.5 rice‑to‑water ratio. Season with herbs, vegetables, and olive oil.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store dry beans in an airtight container in a cool, dry place for up to a year. Keep brown rice in a tightly sealed container in the refrigerator or a dark, cool pantry to prevent the oils from becoming rancid.

broccoli-and-cauliflower-cooked-no-added.title: Broccoli and cauliflower, cooked, no added fat

content.title: About
content.content: Broccoli and cauliflower are two cruciferous vegetables rich in vitamins, minerals, and dietary fiber. When steamed or boiled without added fat they retain most of their nutrients and have a mild, tender flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Broccoli is often called a “super‑vegetable” because of its high glucoraphanin content, a compound with potential anti‑cancer effects.
Cauliflower gets its name from the resemblance of its curd to a flower head.
Both vegetables are excellent sources of vitamin C: 100 g of broccoli provides over 90 % of the daily value, cauliflower about 70 %.
Their fiber content supports a healthy gut microbiome.
Cooking without fat keeps the calorie count low—about 30 kcal per 100 g.

items.title: Immune support
items.content: Vitamin C and antioxidants help strengthen the immune system and combat free radicals.

items.title: Bone health
items.content: Calcium, vitamin K, and magnesium contribute to strong bones.

items.title: Reduced risk of chronic disease
items.content: Phytochemicals such as sulforaphane may lower inflammation and decrease the risk of heart disease.

items.title: Digestive health
items.content: Dietary fiber promotes regular bowel movements and a healthy gut.

items.title: Weight management
items.content: Low calories and high satiety help control appetite.

items.title: Gas and bloating
items.content: Cruciferous vegetables can cause gas in people with sensitive digestion.

items.title: Thyroid interaction
items.content: Large amounts of raw broccoli may affect iodine absorption, but the risk is minimal when cooked.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Rarely, individuals may be allergic to broccoli or cauliflower.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve as a side dish, add to salads, soups, or casseroles. Steam for 5‑7 minutes to keep a slight crunch and preserve nutrients. Season with lemon juice, herbs, or a pinch of salt if desired.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep in the refrigerator in an airtight container for up to 5 days. For longer storage, blanch 2‑3 minutes and freeze in portion‑size bags.

content.title: About
content.content: Pickled cauliflower consists of small cauliflower florets that are cured in a brine of vinegar, spices, and sometimes sugar. It has a crisp texture and a tangy, aromatic flavor that makes it a popular snack and addition to many dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Pickled cauliflower is widely used in Asian cuisines, especially Korean and Japanese dishes.
The vegetable is rich in vitamin C, and the pickling process retains most of this vitamin.
There are many brine variations, from classic vinegar to soy‑soy sauce with ginger and garlic.
It can serve as a milder alternative to sauerkraut in some recipes.
In several countries it is served as part of an appetizer platter alongside olives and cheese.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C supports the immune system and aids collagen synthesis.

items.title: Contains dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber promotes healthy digestion and helps you feel full.

items.title: Low‑calorie food
items.content: Pickled cauliflower is low in calories, making it suitable for weight‑management diets.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Phytonutrients in cauliflower help combat free radicals.

items.title: Supports bone health
items.content: Cauliflower provides vitamin K and small amounts of calcium, both important for bones.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Pickled foods often contain a lot of salt, which can raise blood pressure if consumed in excess.

items.title: Cauliflower allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to cauliflower or its brine.

items.title: Vinegar acidity
items.content: Vinegar can irritate the stomach in people with high acidity.

items.title: Bacterial contamination
items.content: Improper storage may lead to growth of harmful bacteria.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Pickled cauliflower can be enjoyed straight from the jar, added to salads, sandwiches, sushi rolls, or used as a garnish for meat dishes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep refrigerated in a sealed jar. When stored properly, it remains safe and flavorful for 2–3 weeks. Discard if you notice off‑odors or mold.

content.title: About
content.content: Cornbread muffin is a small baked good made from cornmeal, often offered as an individual muffin, a stick, or a round roll. It has a soft, slightly crumbly texture, a golden crust, and a mildly sweet‑savory flavor with distinct corn notes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Cornbread muffins are especially popular in the United States, particularly in Southern states where corn is a staple crop.
Traditional recipes use buttermilk or kefir, which keep the crumb moist and flavorful.
Variations may include cheese, bacon, green onions, or sweet additions such as honey and berries.
Cornmeal is naturally gluten‑free, making these muffins suitable for people with celiac disease when no wheat flour is added.
The corn aroma intensifies when the muffins are baked with steam.

items.title: Source of dietary fiber
items.content: Cornmeal provides fiber that supports digestion and promotes satiety.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Cornbread muffins contain thiamine, niacin, and folate, which are important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Compared with many wheat‑based muffins, corn versions typically contain less saturated fat.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Corn provides lutein and zeaxanthin, nutrients beneficial for eye health.

items.title: Gluten‑free when made with pure cornmeal
items.content: Suitable for those avoiding gluten, provided no wheat flour is used.

items.title: Corn allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to corn products.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Corn‑based baked goods can raise blood sugar quickly, so people with diabetes should consume them in moderation.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Store‑bought muffins often contain added salt; those monitoring sodium intake should check the label.

items.title: Preservatives in commercial versions
items.content: Mass‑produced muffins may contain additives and preservatives that some consumers prefer to avoid.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cornbread muffins can be enjoyed warm or at room temperature, as a snack on their own, with butter, honey, jam, or cream cheese. They pair well with soups, salads, or as part of a breakfast plate.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep muffins in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 3 days. For longer storage, refrigerate up to 1 week or freeze in bags for up to 3 months. Reheat in the oven or microwave before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Fried cod is a member of the cod family prepared by deep‑frying or pan‑frying with a small amount of oil. It has tender white flesh, a mildly sweet flavor, and a crispy crust after cooking. The product is commonly served as fillets, patties, or sticks.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Cod is one of the most widely caught commercial fish in the North Atlantic and the North Sea.
Cod meat is high in protein and low in fat, making it popular in diet nutrition.
Cod can change the color of its skin depending on the environment, helping it hide from predators.
In Russia, fried cod is often served with mashed potatoes, sauerkraut, or tartar sauce.
Cod can grow over 1.5 m in length, though most catches are 60–80 cm long.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Fried cod provides about 18 g of protein per 100 g, supporting muscle maintenance.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: When fried with a modest amount of oil, cod remains relatively low‑calorie.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Cod contains vitamin B12, niacin, and vitamin B6, important for metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: The fish supplies selenium, iodine, and phosphorus, which support thyroid function and bone health.

items.title: Omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: Although lower than fatty fish, cod still contributes omega‑3s that benefit cardiovascular health.

items.title: Fish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to seafood, including cod.

items.title: Heavy metal content
items.content: Cod can accumulate small amounts of mercury and other metals; moderate consumption is advised.

items.title: High‑calorie frying
items.content: Frying in large amounts of oil significantly increases the dish’s calorie count.

items.title: Foodborne infections
items.content: Undercooked fillet may contain pathogenic bacteria; ensure thorough cooking.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Fried cod can be served as a standalone dish, in fillet form, as patties, or sticks. It pairs well with lemon, tartar sauce, mayonnaise, fresh vegetables, or a potato side. For a lighter option, use whole‑grain breadcrumbs for the coating.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked fried cod in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2‑3 days. For longer storage, freeze in the freezer for up to 2 months, sealing the package to remove air.

oatmeal-instant-maple-flavored-no-added-.title: Instant Oatmeal, Maple Flavor, No Added Fat

content.title: About
content.content: Instant oatmeal with maple flavor and no added fat is a quick‑dissolving breakfast ready in one minute of hot water. The oats are pre‑steamed and finely cut, while the maple taste comes from natural extracts. No added oil makes it a low‑calorie option.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Oats are one of the oldest cultivated grains, grown by humans for over 5,000 years.
Instant oatmeal retains most of the fiber and beta‑glucans found in whole oat kernels.
Maple flavor is often derived from real maple syrup or natural flavorings without added sugar.
Oats contain avenanthramides, compounds that may support heart health.
Instant oat packets are popular for travel and camping because they require no cooking equipment.

items.title: Rich in beta‑glucans
items.content: Beta‑glucans help lower cholesterol and support immune function.

items.title: Source of complex carbs
items.content: Oats provide sustained energy and a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Contains iron and magnesium
items.content: These minerals are essential for blood formation and normal muscle function.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: The absence of added fat makes it suitable for calorie‑controlled diets.

items.title: High in antioxidants
items.content: Avenanthramides and phenolic compounds protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Oat allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to oats or the gluten-like proteins they contain.

items.title: Gluten cross‑contamination
items.content: Oats are often processed on equipment shared with wheat, so gluten contamination is possible.

items.title: Maple flavor sweetener
items.content: Although fat‑free, the maple flavor may include a small amount of sugar; people monitoring blood glucose should check the label.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Pour 250 ml of boiling water over the packet, stir, and let sit for 1–2 minutes. Add fresh berries, nuts, seeds, or a dollop of yogurt for extra nutrition.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the unopened package in a dry, cool place away from moisture. Once opened, consume within 3–4 weeks to maintain flavor and texture.

pasta-with-tomato-based-sauce-and-added-.title: Pasta with Tomato-Based Sauce and Vegetables

content.title: About
content.content: Pasta with tomato-based sauce and added vegetables is a home recipe where cooked pasta is tossed with a sauce made from tomatoes, aromatic herbs, and a mix of vegetables such as bell pepper, zucchini, carrot, and spinach. The dish is rich in vitamins, minerals, and fiber, providing lasting satiety.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Tomato sauce is an excellent source of lycopene, a powerful antioxidant that becomes more bioavailable after cooking.
Combining pasta with vegetables boosts fiber intake without significantly increasing calories.
In traditional Italian cuisine, pasta is often served with a “Marinara” sauce made from tomatoes, garlic, and olive oil.
Adding spinach to the sauce raises the iron and vitamin K content.
Quick preparation (about 30 minutes) makes this dish popular among busy people.

items.title: Rich in lycopene
items.content: Cooked tomatoes provide high levels of lycopene, which supports heart health and may reduce the risk of certain cancers.

items.title: High fiber content
items.content: Vegetables and whole‑grain pasta supply dietary fiber that promotes healthy digestion and stable blood sugar.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals
items.content: Bell pepper, carrot, and spinach add vitamin C, vitamin A, folate, and iron, essential for immunity and vision.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Preparing the sauce with olive oil makes the dish more heart‑friendly compared with heavy cream‑based sauces.

items.title: Satiety support
items.content: The combination of complex carbs from pasta and protein from vegetables helps keep you full longer.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Traditional pasta contains wheat, which can trigger reactions in people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Store‑bought tomato sauce can be salty; monitor added salt to keep sodium intake moderate.

items.title: Acidity of tomatoes
items.content: For some individuals, the acidic sauce may cause heartburn or stomach discomfort.

items.title: Portion size
items.content: Pasta is easy to overeat; keep portions moderate, especially when managing weight.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve hot, sprinkled with grated Parmesan or vegan cheese if desired. Add fresh basil, a drizzle of olive oil, or a pinch of red pepper flakes for extra flavor. The dish stores well in the refrigerator for up to 3 days and can be reheated in the microwave or on the stovetop.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the cooked pasta in an airtight container in the refrigerator for no more than 3 days. For longer storage, freeze portions in freezer bags for up to 2 months. Reheat to an internal temperature of at least 75 °C before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Pinto beans (Phaseolus vulgaris) are a widely cultivated variety of bean native to the Americas. They have a light‑brown speckled appearance, a soft texture when cooked, and a mildly nutty, slightly sweet flavor. Pinto beans are commonly used in soups, stews, chili, and as a side dish.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The name “pinto” comes from the Spanish word for “spotted.”
Pinto beans are a key ingredient in the Mexican dish “frijoles refritos” and are popular in Southwestern U.S. cuisine.
Their high starch content makes them an excellent thickener for sauces and soups.
In the United States, pinto beans rank among the top five most consumed bean varieties.
They are a good source of plant protein and fiber, making them valuable for vegetarians.

items.title: Rich in plant protein
items.content: A 100‑g serving of cooked pinto beans provides about 9 g of protein, supporting muscle maintenance.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber promotes healthy digestion, helps regulate blood sugar, and increases satiety.

items.title: Contains iron and magnesium
items.content: These minerals are essential for blood formation and normal nerve function.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: Pinto beans raise blood glucose slowly, which is beneficial for people with pre‑diabetes.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Phytochemicals such as polyphenols help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Phytic acid
items.content: Present in legumes, it can reduce mineral absorption; soaking and cooking mitigate this effect.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: A small number of individuals may experience allergic reactions to beans.

items.title: Gas formation
items.content: Beans can cause increased flatulence; gradual introduction to the diet lessens the issue.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Pinto beans are typically boiled in water for 1.5–2 hours until tender. They are added to chili, soups, salads, purees, and vegetarian patties. Canned beans are convenient, but choose varieties without added salt or preservatives.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store dry pinto beans in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place for up to 1 year. Cooked beans keep in the refrigerator for 3–4 days and can be frozen for up to 6 months.
